blocks.p: The price sticker was still on the back. Three hundred and eighty yen, half peeled off, curling up at one corner. It must have curled like that for months, every time Gin opened the drawer.

Third drawer. Under the charger. The voice on the voicemail had been almost nothing, almost Gin, and it had been right. Rei went into Gin's room, opened the third drawer of the desk, and lifted the phone charger. Underneath it lay a cheap notebook with a brown paper cover, the kind sold in any konbini. It was soft at the spine from being bent back. He held it as if it might be hot.

He did not sit in Gin's chair. The chair felt like it belonged to someone who was coming back, and he could not bear to take it. So he sat on the floor beside the desk with his back against the drawers.

Outside the window, more Obon lanterns were going up along the canal. Each one was a small paper box with a light inside, there to show the visiting dead the way home. Rei looked at the soft lights and thought that they were not meant for whatever was walking around in his brother now.

He opened the notebook to the first page. The hand was Gin's. It was the small, cramped writing Gin had had since he was nine. It leaned to the left, as if it were trying to take up less room than it had been given.

He read forward. The early entries were the entries of a tired man. A case that closed too easily. A name that was in no file. Gin's instruments showing the veil over Kita ward getting thinner, when those instruments should not have been able to measure it at all. Gin was frightened in these pages. But it was an ordinary fear. It was the fear of a man who suspects he is right about something and would give anything to be wrong.

Between the cases were the small lines Gin always wrote at the bottom of a page to sign off. Rei had seen a hundred of them in the big Archive on the desk. Keys on the hook. Coffee terrible. Rei took the umbrella. Good. Here, in the cheap notebook, the small lines had begun to change.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Undated. Early.
lines: Coffee made before I remembered making it.
The apartment is starting to feel smaller than it used to. I do not think this is about the apartment.

blocks.p: Rei read that twice. He knew about the coffee. On more than one morning that summer he had come out of his room and found a full pot already going cold. Gin would be standing beside it with a faintly puzzled face, as though the pot had made itself. Rei had laughed at him. He did not laugh now. A man who makes coffee without remembering he made it has lost a few minutes somewhere. Gin had noticed. He had written it down. And then he had gone on with his day.

doc.title: Gin's journal. A Thursday.
lines: End of a long week. Something in the building across the street has been watching the window since Tuesday.
I have been noting it without addressing it, which is unlike me.
I have three theories. I am proceeding on the most comfortable one.

blocks.p: Rei got up and went to the window. Across the street stood a block of small flats with dark balconies. On the third floor an air conditioner unit dripped water onto the balcony below. Futons hung over two of the railings. Nothing looked back at him. He stood there until he felt foolish. Then he stood there a little longer, because Gin had never been a man who felt watched for no reason.
A few pages later the watcher came back into the journal. And so did something worse.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Several days later.
lines: The thing across the street did not return after that first week. I have stopped noting its absence.
The thing across the street was not Rei. I have not fully resolved what it was. I have chosen not to pursue it further.
The reason. I am tired this week in a way that is not entirely accounted for by the caseload.

blocks.p: Was not Rei. Gin had checked whether the thing watching the window was his own brother. Rei understood why. His own gift ran loud. Gin had told him so in a dozen careful ways over the years, and Rei had always heard them as complaints about the mess in the kitchen. So when Gin felt pressure on the window, his first question was whether it was only Rei, leaking through the wall. It was not. And Gin had decided to let it go, because he was too tired to chase it.
Rei made himself keep reading.

blocks.break: The thing he thought was watching

blocks.p: Halfway through the notebook, Gin had copied out a few lines from a secret part of the big Archive. He had given that page a caption. The thing the framework will not name.

The page described something the Directorate's researchers called the Architect Phenomenon. In plain words, the Architect was not a ghost, a person or a group. It was the veil's own slow answer to a practitioner who hid a large rank for years and never let it out. The veil seemed to notice the hidden weight, the way a scale notices a hand pressing on it. Then, over time, it pushed back. The page listed what happened to such people in the end. Their hidden power burst out of them by force. Or they became easy to possess. Or they disappeared, or died. Now and then one survived and ended up in some strange new role. And the person being watched usually knew. The page said the Architect's attention felt like a very particular kind of being watched.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Underneath.
lines: I have been aware of my status for approximately three years.

It is not threatening in the way an entity's attention is threatening. It is more like the feeling of a very large system becoming aware of a very small irregularity. Patient. Inevitable. Not personal.
I find this more frightening than I would find something personal. Personal things can be negotiated with. This cannot.
If you are a suppressor, if you have been masking your level, you should know that the math eventually balances. Not as threat. As information.

blocks.p: Rei knew what Gin was. On paper Gin was a Ritualist, a grade C. He had been measured as a C for six years while he held something much larger underneath. That was the Uedera habit. Stay sloppy. Stay unremarkable. Gin had taught it to Rei at the kitchen table before Rei could read. So when Gin began to feel watched by something huge and patient, he reached for the only explanation his training gave him. The veil itself had noticed what he was hiding. It was coming, slowly, to balance the books.

Rei sat on the floor with the notebook on his knees and felt that explanation wobble. Earlier that night he had read another page of Gin's, in the chapter on demons, and one line of it would not leave him alone. Demons produce directional membrane thinning around their location. The thinning points toward rather than radiating from. In simple words, a demon does not weaken the veil evenly all around, like a lamp lighting a room. It weakens it in a line, pointing at the thing it wants. The Architect, Gin had written, was a system. It was not personal. But the thing across the street had not watched the whole district. It had watched one window.
Rei did not know yet what that meant. He put a pencil mark beside the Architect page and went on.

blocks.cap: The Kita thin spot from Observation Log 7-C

blocks.p: Near the middle of the notebook there was a folder note, copied across from the big Archive. A small piece of tape was stuck to its corner. Gin had always taped the folders he did not trust, so he could see if anyone opened them.

The note was about a thin spot. A thin spot is a place where the veil between the living and the dead has worn weak, the way cloth wears thin at the knee. There are thin spots all over Tokyo. Most are small. The one in Kita was not small.

doc.title: Observation Log 7-C. Kita thin spot
lines: Three anchor signatures in a pattern around the Kita thin spot. I have been documenting them for eight months.
I put a small piece of tape on the folder and checked.
Rei has walked past the thin spot twelve times in the last month. I've counted. I'm counting.

blocks.cap: The CVD Research Division, where the stability mapping was done

blocks.p: Under the folder note Gin had pasted a copy of a research page. It came from the Division's own laboratories, and it was stamped for Protocol eyes only.

doc.title: CVD Research Division. Veil Stability Mapping Project. Phase III. Protocol Eyes Only
lines: Veil Stability Anchor Signatures. Open research question.

Phase III identified anomalous stability signatures globally, points where the membrane is reinforced rather than thinned, in ways no geographic or practitioner-density model predicts. The report calls them self-organizing reinforcement nodes. The practitioners who work near them call them the warm spots.
The signatures correlate with specific emotional registers in surrounding human and entity populations. They have been continuously active for longer than the project's historical data reaches.
Practitioners operating in the influence radius of an anchor signature show subtle stability variations the standard mapping does not predict. Mechanism unconfirmed.

blocks.p: Rei read it slowly. Most of the city's thin spots were cold wounds in the veil. But the researchers had found the opposite too. There were a few places in the world where the veil was stronger than it should be, as if something were holding it closed. The scientists called them reinforcement nodes. The field officers called them warm spots. Nobody knew what made them.

Gin's caption under the page said only The same room. Very different weather. Three warm spots around one cold wound. And his little brother walking past the wound twelve times a month without knowing it was there. Rei knew exactly which way that was. It was the short cut to the konbini by the river. He had walked it because it was quicker.
Then he reached the entry dated the fourteenth of August. It was three lines long, and it stopped in the middle of a sentence.

doc.title: Gin's journal. 14 August.
lines: Long shift. Walked home alone, late, the dense way along the canal, because I could not face the train.
Rei's light was on under his door when I got in. Did not eat. Did not knock.
I need to sleep before I

blocks.p: The next page was dated the same night, an hour later. The handwriting had changed.

It had not changed wildly. That was the part that got into him and stayed. It had only become a little more even. A little more upright. It was as if someone had studied Gin's writing for an afternoon and then, being a careful student, written it back to Rei slightly improved.

Rei sat with that for a long time while the lantern light moved on the wall. He was looking at the exact hour. Two pages, one man on either side. His hands were cold. He wanted very badly to close the book and tell himself it was only grief, making patterns out of nothing.

But he had read enough of Gin's casework to know one thing. When a person wants to un-see something, that wish is exactly what the thing is counting on. So he turned the page, into the entries the new hand had written.

In the margins were small numbers, neat and calm, like the numbers a librarian writes on the spine of a book. They told him the order to read the entries in. If he followed them, the journal stopped being a diary and became an argument, beautifully arranged.

First came the dead of 2011, who had never been given their rites. Next came the veil over Kita, which had been weeping for them ever since. After that came one empty seat at the table of the Thirteen. It had been empty for a long time. Long enough, the entries said, that it could become the cure for all that weeping. All it needed was someone with the right grade and the right wound, who would agree to feel the duty.

None of it was a lie. That was what kept making him put the book down. Each entry was a true thing. It was only the order that was wrong. Each true thing was laid on the last one a little crooked, so the whole pile leaned one way. Somewhere around the ninth page, Rei caught himself nodding. The nod was the price.

He had thought he would be fighting something. Instead he was only listening, and listening leaves marks. Slowly he learned to tell the two writers apart. He did it by the feeling under each line, by what each line wanted from him.

Gin's own entries, the ones in the old leftward hand, grew fewer with every page. They wanted him to stop. They were clumsy. They repeated themselves. They said go home in four different broken ways. They read like a man trying to shout through a wall while someone held his hand.

The other entries were calm, and they wanted him closer. They wanted him to understand. They reasoned with him the way a person reasons with a frightened animal they mean to keep. The worst of it was how good the reasoning was. On a clearer night he might almost have signed his name under it.

An hour in, he noticed that he had started to think in the same rhythm as the new hand. When he reached for an objection of his own, it came to him already softened. It came already in the new hand's order, as if it had been given its own small number in the margin. His body felt it as a kind of seasickness. The floor of his own mind was tilting a few degrees, toward a shape that was not his.

Gin had a word for that. Gin had a whole chapter for it. Twice he had left that chapter open on the kitchen table, and both times Rei had closed it without reading it. Now he reached up, pulled the big Archive down off the desk, and found it. On the first page, in Gin's margin, was a short note.

doc.title: Chapter Five. Gin's margin note
lines: Three readings. Never confuse them.
Health is the body, and only the body takes it. A blow, a fall, a ridden host's hands.
Stability is the anchor that holds you closed against the veil. It is what power and dread spend, and what the dead lean on. As it falls the membrane opens. At zero you are wide open.
Madness is the slow corruption pooling. It climbs when the veil gets in, above all through broken Stability, and it does not wash out.
A practitioner ends one of two ways and they are not the same death. The body fails. Or the self does. The anchor breaks, Madness fills, and something else moves into the empty room.
Rank and Stability are two separate axes. Rank is what you can do. Stability is whether doing it ends you.

blocks.p: Rei read the note twice, and then he put it into his own words, so he would keep it. A person had three things that could break. Health was the body. Stability was the lock on the door between him and the veil. Every use of power cost some of it, and so did fear, and so did the dead leaning on him. Madness was what came in through that door once it stood open, and Madness did not leave again. Rank was how strong a person was. Stability was whether that strength would end him.
So that was the tilt. It was not Madness. Not yet. It was his Stability, spending itself a little with every page he turned.

His hand was already closing the journal. He watched it do that, the way a person watches their own foot step back from the edge of a train platform. It would be so easy to stop. He would sleep. He would wake up knowing less and feeling better. And his brother would still be a smooth voice on the phone.
He thought of Gin at this same desk, writing a chapter he knew Rei would close twice without reading. Writing it anyway.
Rei opened the journal again at the page where he had stopped.
In the end it was not something horrible that gave the thing away. It was something kind.

Near the back, in the even upright hand, there was an entry about Rei. It was warm. It remembered the summer Rei broke his wrist, and how Gin had carried his school bag for a month. It used the small pet name that only Gin ever used. Rei was reading it with a tight throat, almost grateful, when the seasickness saved him.

He had read this exact warmth before. It was in Gin's casework, forty pages earlier, in the old leftward hand. It was the section where Gin wrote about how to tell a person who has been worn by a demon from a person who is still whole. Rei turned back and found it.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Casework. The old hand.
lines: What it cannot calibrate is the direction of the warmth. It orients toward whoever is currently useful, rather than toward whoever the host actually cared about.
This is the tell. It has saved my life twice and I am not being dramatic about that.
The tell is never the warmth itself. It is the direction the warmth points. A demon keeps the host's whole register of affection and aims all of it at whoever is useful now.

blocks.p: Rei read the entry about the broken wrist again, with that rule in his head. It was not love remembering him. It was love being aimed at him.

Now he understood what he had been swimming in for three hours, and why it had worked so well on him. It was Gin's warmth, measured exactly right. And it was pointed at Rei because Rei was the pair of hands it wanted. Gin's real entries never aimed at anything. They stumbled toward him, repeating themselves, useless, asking for nothing. They only wanted him to live.

That was how he would tell them apart from now on. In every text, in every short window when Gin broke through, in every reasonable favour still to come. Not by something sounding wrong, because the thing could smooth that away. By the direction of the wanting. Gin wanted him safe and gone. The thing wanted him near and helpful. The voice that wanted something from him was never the voice that loved him, however perfectly it had learned to sound as if it did.

Rei closed the journal. The lantern light had climbed all the way up the wall. Out on the canal, people were setting paper lanterns on the black water. Each one floated away slowly with its small flame, a way of wishing the dead a safe road back. Rei would not get to do that for Gin tonight. Maybe never. The last three hours sat in him like cold water at the base of his spine. He could feel clearly the few degrees by which his inner floor had not come back to level.
But he knew the seam now. He could hear where the thing ended and where his brother began. It was the first tool he had been given that the thing could not take back just by being reasonable.
He set the journal on the desk beside the big Archive. He looked at the two of them lying together, and something about the picture bothered him.

A neighbour had seen a man wearing Gin's face fit a key to this door. Whoever that was had stood in this room, at this desk, while Rei was out. He had left the lamp on. He had left the Archive open, six years of Gin's writing about exactly what he was. And he had left the journal in its drawer, with the seam inside it and the warmth that pointed the wrong way, for anyone to find.

A careful thing does not leave evidence lying on a desk. Rei could not think why it would. He wrote the question in pencil on the inside cover of the journal, small, so he would not forget it. Why didn't it burn these?
Then he pulled the lamp down onto the floor, opened the Archive at the chapter Gin had told him to read twice, and began.
